attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his post, stated as fact. The proposition covers only part (a) of the sentence.

semantics.note: Faithful to clause (a), which is stated firmly as fact. The separate profitability clause is correctly left out.

contract.note: Reading 'many applications' as several substantial application classes, with consequential failures, is an ordinary and fair plain reading. It is not stretched for or against the speaker.

evidence.note: Legal benchmark dated Nov 18, 2026. It spans many areas of practice. Under 40% of attempts pass a strict threshold, and wrong conclusions have serious client consequences.
Regulatory-affairs benchmark completed Nov 4, 2026. The best system fully passes about 29% of tasks, which shows a second application class with frequent failures.

reviews.rationale: Two November 2026 benchmarks show frequent failures against professional standards in two substantial application classes: law across many practice areas, and regulatory affairs. This meets the support condition. The packet lists no counterevidence. The gaps it notes, such as no census of all uses, do not undercut 'many applications'.

attribution.note: Marcus's own retrospective assertion, which also refers to his own 2024 prediction.

semantics.note: This is a retrospective comparative claim plus a claim that he predicted it. Both parts are kept.

contract.note: The contract fairly notes that 'helped more' has no common measure and that 'other domains' is ambiguous, for example whether coding counts. The result depends on these readings, which the speaker did not supply.

evidence.note: Marcus's own Nov 2024 post guessed that o1 test-time scaling would work best in closed domains like math. This is a related but narrower and hedged earlier position. It cannot prove the later comparison.
Shows math gains from Lean-grounded reinforcement learning (AlphaProof). It has no comparison across domains.
Shows that math-tuned provers transfer poorly to software verification. This is a narrow transfer finding, not a ranking of benefits across domains.
Reports gains in both math and coding over a verifiable-rewards baseline. It does not rank the domains, so it neither supports nor contradicts the claim.

reviews.rationale: No item in the packet compares gains attributable to verification across domains on a common basis. The math gains (e2) and the poor transfer to software (e3) fit the claim loosely. Gains in coding (e4) muddy it if coding counts as an 'other domain'. The 2024 record is related but narrower. The evidence does not settle the claim.

attribution.note: Marcus's own firm assertion in his post.

semantics.note: Faithful. The praise of Alpöge is rightly treated as non-measurable.

contract.note: Reading 'required' as describing the workflow that actually produced the result, not proven counterfactual necessity, is an ordinary and testable reading. 'Extensive' is reasonably read as substantial, repeated mathematical direction.

evidence.note: Quanta, Nov 20, 2026: Alpöge's expertise played a major role in repeated, iterative attempts with Claude. This rests on Alpöge's own account and corroborates it, but it is not an independent audit.

reviews.rationale: Contemporaneous specialist reporting describes substantial, repeated mathematical direction from Alpöge across the development process. This meets the support condition. No evidence shows autonomous production. Claude's large late-stage contribution does not contradict extensive human guidance. The participant source (remark.pdf) is listed as used, but no evidence item for it was supplied.

attribution.note: Marcus's own observation about Anthropic stock.

semantics.note: Keeps 'after hours' and 'much'. The causal claim that 'the market gets it' is rightly separated from the price observation.

contract.note: A fair plain reading: a small after-hours move after the Friday Nov 20 announcement, judged against volatility. 'Much' has no threshold, so interpretation matters.

evidence.note: The Public snapshot is internally inconsistent. Its table shows Nov 20 after hours at -0.65%, but the FAQ labels the session Nov 21, a Saturday, at +1.50% from a different close. It cannot reliably set the Friday after-hours response.

reviews.rationale: The only evidence is a brokerage snapshot whose session date and reference close conflict. No reconciled after-hours series aligned to the announcement time was obtained. Both of its figures hint at a small move, but the basis is unreliable, so the claim cannot be settled.
